source.title: LinguaLens: Towards Interpreting Linguistic Mechanisms of Large Language Models via Sparse Auto-Encoder
source.authors: Yi Jing; Zi-Jun Yao; Hong-Zhu Guo; Ling-Xu Ran; Xiaozhi Wang; Lei Hou; Juan-Zi Li

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes linguistic features in an LLM using SAE extraction and interventions, providing indirect evidence about SAE-recoverable features in a real model rather than testing toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper measures SAE feature extraction, feature specificity, and effects of intervening on selected features. It does not test feature competition under dimensional limits, toy-model superposition geometry, or whether polysemanticity follows from capacity pressure. Cited claims about SAEs and neuron polysemanticity are not treated as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study uses OpenSAE dictionaries on Llama-3.1-8B. It reports that SAE latents track specific linguistic phenomena, with near-zero activation on control constructions, and that steering them partly changes outputs. This is a new-setting result on V4's 'contains sparse features an SAE can recover'. It does not examine neuron-level distribution, capacity, toy geometry, canonicity or dimensionality. The evidence for V4 is weak: it rests on post-selection specificity checks and judge-scored steering, with no statistics.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SAE latents in Llama-3.1-8B encode structured linguistic knowledge, show cross-layer and cross-lingual patterns, and can steer outputs. They claim all six features show 'clear causal effects', yet concede that single interventions are weak or unstable, are inferior to fine-tuning, and are confounded by output quality.
record.recipe_differences: Uses OpenSAE features, counterfactual linguistic datasets, FRC ranking, LLM-assisted interpretation, and feature interventions in an LLM; it does not use the toy-network superposition experiments or geometric measurements of the original work.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences across linguistic domains, Chinese and English, and layers; intervention outcomes vary by feature and by enhancement versus ablation. Joint-intervention results depend on the number of vectors, and the authors identify output quality as a confound for the GPT-4o judge.

fits_no_version.finding: Several SAE latents in the same layer are tied to one linguistic feature (four each for simile and politeness at layer 26). Steering more of them jointly gives no significant gain over random-control trends.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM SAEs, a single linguistic phenomenon is spread over multiple redundant latents, and ablating one is compensated by others.

fits_no_version.finding: The overlap of SAE latents between Chinese and English for matched features is higher at the semantic and pragmatic levels and in layers 0–15.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents for linguistic functions are partly shared across languages, depending on linguistic level and layer.

record.code_released: THU-KEG/LinguaLens (repository identifier stated; URL not stated)
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2025
record.problems: All experiments use Llama-3.1-8B. The paper reports approximately 50 sentence pairs per feature and notes limitations in feature count and dataset size. Intervention success rates are judged by GPT-4o; the authors say random-control rates can be confounded by output quality. No error bars or p-values are reported in the presented results, despite a statement that intervention effects are statistically significant.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Table 1 is recorded as domain-by-language aggregates. Table 2 displays five feature rows in the supplied text although the paper says six representative features were selected; no result for an unshown sixth feature was inferred.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity sweeps or geometry.
All: capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features are not examined.
All: neuron polysemanticity is only cited (Yan et al.), not measured.
Whether features are spread across many neurons (no neuron-level analysis). Only one model and one SAE family (OpenSAE, TopK k=128). No reconstruction or dictionary-quality metrics.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE latents are not tested. Only the top-FRC vectors for selected features are examined.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features are not tested.

missing.what: Cross-lingual latent overlap per layer and feature pair (24 Chinese–English feature sets). The record has no row, and rows_left_out does not declare it.
Layer-wise activation of referent and tenor latents for reference and metaphor sentences.
Four-stage cross-layer distribution of linguistic latents.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is borderline toward T4: SAEs are used as the analysis tool, and most numbers describe the study's own selected latents. Table 1 is selection-dependent, so it is excluded from the verdicts. The paper says six features were intervened on, but Table 2 shows five. It claims statistical significance but reports no tests or error bars. It is unclear whether the Table 5 'self' sentences overlap with the selection data.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more features than dimensions, sparse co-activation, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, and sparsity-dependent geometric transitions.
Whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise without capacity pressure.
The study tests SAE recovery and intervention for linguistic features in Llama-3.1-8B, but does not measure feature distribution across neurons or test other LLMs.
The study assesses selected SAE features for specificity and behavioral effects, but does not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The study does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Jointly intervened on increasing numbers of SAE vectors associated with a feature.

conditions.value: 200 enhancement and 200 ablation experiments per feature

rows.measure: Change in intervention success rates as more vectors are jointly intervened on
rows.value: figure only; the text says success rates of both targeted and control enhancement decreased and both targeted and control ablation increased, while the feature intervention effect did not change significantly after background influences were excluded
rows.note: The authors attribute the shared trend in targeted and control experiments to output-quality effects and report only limited improvement from joint intervention.
rows.check: Figure only. It reports whether joint steering of several latents improves efficacy, which doesn't bear on the existence of SAE-recoverable features. The text says the layer is 26 for both features, although politeness's main vector is at layer 31.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Manually inspected outputs after enhancing or ablating one simile-related SAE vector.

conditions.value: winter description without an explicit simile request; love description with an explicit simile request

rows.measure: Qualitative presence of similes in generated outputs
rows.value: Enhancement produced a simile in the winter case; ablation led to straightforward descriptions without similes in the prompted love case; enhancement retained similes
rows.note: A small manual case study; one condition explicitly prompted the model to use a simile.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B, OpenSAE latents selected for linguistic features (specificity checks and the stronger steering cases)
relationships.reason: Selected latents fire on 74–80/80 target sentences and 0/80 on all listed control constructions (R9–R23). Enhancement beats random latents by a clear margin for linking verb, simile and politeness, and politeness ablation also clearly beats its control (R28, R36, R40, R42). A qualitative simile case agrees (R46). Specificity is measured only after selection, and no significance tests are given.
relationships.display_finding: Selected latents fired on 74–80 of 80 target sentences and on none of the listed control constructions. Enhancing them clearly beat random latents for linking verb, simile and politeness, and politeness ablation also beat its control, though specificity was measured only after selection and no significance tests were given.

source_check.condition: Llama-3.1-8B, OpenSAE latents selected for linguistic features (specificity checks and the stronger steering cases)
source_check.reason: R9–R23 show selected latents activating on target constructions with zero activation on listed controls; R28, R36, R40 and R42 provide additional intervention evidence for the recovered interpretations.

relationships.condition: Single-latent causal interventions judged by GPT-4o (past tense, causality, linking-verb ablation, simile ablation)
relationships.reason: For past tense and causality, and for linking-verb ablation, targeted effects are only 4–12 points above random controls (R24, R26, R30, R32, R34). Simile ablation falls below its control (R38). The authors say single-latent effects are weak and confounded by output quality, so recovered latents are not reliably causal on their own.
relationships.display_finding: Targeted effects for past tense, causality and linking-verb ablation were only 4–12 points above random controls, and simile ablation fell below its control. The authors say single-latent effects are weak and confounded by output quality.

source_check.reason: These results limit reliable control by individual latents. V4 asserts distributed or SAE-recoverable features and does not require reliable single-latent control; weak or reversed steering does not demonstrate a failure of feature recovery.
